checks.name: Runs test (is the sequence random?)
checks.detail: 15,837 runs vs 15,303 expected (z = +6.11, p = 0.000): more switches than chance: results tend to alternate. Check that it also holds out of sample.

checks.name: Does one result predict the next?
checks.detail: lag-1 correlation -0.0349 (z = -6.11). Statistically non-zero, but check its size: a correlation this small moves the next window's odds by only about 1.7 percentage points, less than fees cost.

checks.name: Hour-of-day lean holds out of sample?
checks.detail: Split at 2026-06-20. Hours that looked significant in the first half: 13:00; still significant, same direction, in the second half: none. Correlation of hourly leans between halves: -0.23 (near zero: the hourly pattern is noise).

checks.name: Streak behaviour holds out of sample?
checks.detail: after 3 Ups the next was Up 46.3% (first half, n=1,681) vs 47.5% (second half, n=1,763); after 3 Downs the next was Up 53.9% (first half, n=1,700) vs 53.6% (second half, n=1,786). For a fade-or-follow rule to pay, the same lean must show in both halves and be larger than the ~2–3¢ per contract that spread and fees cost.

checks.name: Kalshi price edge holds out of sample?
checks.detail: 1 price level looked clearly profitable in the first half (buy Yes at 70–80¢) but did not hold up in the second. 7 more showed a paper profit that sits inside its error band, so it could just be luck: buy No at 40–50¢: +9.2¢ ±10.6 (n=81); buy Yes at 20–30¢: +4.9¢ ±9.3 (n=99); buy No at 60–70¢: +3.6¢ ±12.1 (n=66). Most windows trade under 10¢ or over 90¢; there, recent results ran -0.6¢ to +0.1¢ per contract.

checks.name: Chance findings to expect
checks.detail: The report tests 35 hour, weekday and slot groups; at 95% confidence about 1.8 would look significant by luck alone. Found: 0. That's no more than luck would produce.
